doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Conducting and arranging at Motown
summary: Berry Gordy brought him to Motown as conductor; he could not grasp the Funk Brothers' writing style.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yeah. That’s very interesting again. And you’ve also done some work in I guess you could call it the popular music field with some Motown artists and that kind of thing?

Well that was during the time when the trombone actually was becoming quite unpopular in the States. That was in the sixties after I had played with Dizzy’s band and Art Blakey and you weren’t hearing much about trombones doing any recordings or anything like that. But this guy Berry Gordy and some other people that knew about me because I had worked with Lloyd Price’s band as the musical director, so they wanted me to come out there. Because they actually wanted to start some kind of a jazz label. I don’t think — they said they wanted to start a jazz label, but I don’t think they knew what they really

meant. They didn’t mean the same thing that we might have meant. But when I went out there and I started working as a conductor, I was conducting shows, I was conducting Stevie Wonder and the Four Tops and all of that stuff, and some of the big shows and things. I went into some of the studios where they worked, I went to the studios and they had a way of writing that was really unique. I really — you couldn’t just be a good writer and go out there and take part in that. There was something special they had. And when I went in and listened to it and heard it I said this is something different. This is something that they really feel. That’s the way it developed. So it wasn’t — I wasn’t able to really contribute a lot. I did some arranging in special situations, but I wasn’t able to get in to that stuff that they were writing behind the Supremes and all that. Those guys did that better than anybody.

The group that did all the recording was called The Funk Brothers. That was the rhythm section. They had a lot to do with it because they would get a very simple lead sheet and they would develop the music that we heard out of that lead sheet. But there were some other guys that were writing that — they had several writers that were doing the arrangements. And those guys, there were about four or five guys, and they had a special way of writing that was really wonderful for that music.

Yeah when you listen to like “My Girl,” the way that tune develops and eventually the string parts fit in and they mesh with what has already been going on which just continues throughout the song is really, as you said, pretty special.

There’s some thought that went into it. And it’s with the feeling. It wasn’t only a system, it was a feeling. Because I listened to it and I was trying to see what is this that they’re doing. But I couldn’t really catch it. I guess I didn’t really find it. It’s interesting, that I might have felt when I listened to bebop I had to find out what was going on, so I listened for hours and listened to all the CDs and went over stuff and everything. But there I was listening to see if I could understand that concept. I didn’t, but I did enjoy what they did though.
